results.reply:
The 30‑day window to send a demand notice under s.138 has already passed (deadline was 9 Sept 2026). Because the notice period is missed, filing a criminal complaint under s.138 is now risky – courts may reject it as out of time. You could still try a civil summary suit to recover the ₹85,000, but you’ll need a lawyer to check if it’s viable.

**What you can do next**
- Gather all proof: the bounced‑cheque copy, bank’s return memo (dated 10 Aug 2026), any email/WhatsApp where the customer promised payment, and your bank statements showing the cheque was presented.
- Talk to a lawyer (free legal aid via NALSA 15100 or Tele‑Law) to see if a civil suit or any other remedy is possible.
- If you later manage to send a notice, it may help in settlement, but it won’t revive the criminal route.

citations.title: Cheque bounce offence: conditions and punishment
citations.plain: Bouncing a cheque given to pay a legally enforceable debt, because of insufficient funds or because it exceeds the arranged limit, is a crime. Punishment is up to 2 years' jail, or a fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both. The offence arises only if (a) the cheque was presented within its validity (now 3 months), (b) the payee sent a written demand notice within 30 days of learning it bounced, and (c) the drawer failed to pay within 15 days of receiving that notice.

citations.title: Time limit to file cheque bounce complaint
citations.plain: Only the payee or holder can file, by written complaint. It must be filed within one month after the cause of action arises, which is when the 15-day payment period after the notice ends without payment. A court can accept a late complaint if you show sufficient cause. Only a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate First Class can try the case.

citations.title: Summary suits for fixed money claims
citations.plain: A summary suit is a faster procedure for clear money claims. It covers suits on cheques, bills of exchange, hundis and promissory notes, and suits to recover a fixed debt or 'liquidated' amount (with or without interest) arising from a written contract, a law that fixes the sum, or a guarantee. The defendant may defend only with the court's permission ('leave to defend'). It is available only in courts where the Order applies.
